name: Private State Tokens
plain: Lets one site share a trust signal about a visitor with another without identifying them.
meaning: Carries a one bit trust token to other origins so bots can be told from people without a login. Privacy Sandbox wind down affects its future.

access.iframe: Same as top level; cross-origin iframes need a permissions policy where listed

data.metric: Lets one site share a trust signal about a visitor with another without identifying them.

limits.headline: Can pass a small trust badge about you between sites without naming you
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens quietly in the background when the page loads
can: Store a token after a site decides you are probably a real person
Show that token to another site so it can skip a bot check
Carry one yes or no signal, with no name or account
cannot: Tell the other site who you are
Count on a long future, because Chrome is winding down the Privacy Sandbox
limits.differs: Only Chromium browsers have it. Firefox and Safari do not.

story.what_it_is: A site can pass a hidden 'this is a real person' mark to another site, without your identity.

marketing.name: Private State Tokens
marketing.pitch: Google pitched it as a way for sites to share a trust signal about a visitor across sites without identifying them or using cookies.

story.for_you: You never see it. After you pass a check on one site, the browser may carry a trust token that another site can read as a yes or no. It may mean fewer puzzles asking you to prove you are human.
story.for_makers: Fraud and anti-bot teams want to know a visitor looks like a person before they sign up or buy. The token lets a trusted issuer vouch for the browser, which lowers fake account and ad fraud. The wider Privacy Sandbox project has been scaled back, so its future is unsure.

use_cases.example: A checkout page reads a token from an issuer that earlier saw you act like a normal person, then skips a CAPTCHA for you.
An ad network checks the token to filter out bot clicks and charge advertisers only for real viewers.
A browser game lobby uses the mark to keep bots out of free signups and ranked queues without nagging players.
A social site gates new account creation behind the token, so a bot farm cannot register thousands of accounts.
A ticket seller uses it to let real fans into the queue while keeping scalper bots out.
A measurement vendor keeps traffic counts clean by excluding visits with no trust mark.

risks: Might label some real people as bots

technical_bounds: Limit of about 2 issuers per origin in Chrome

abuse: Cross site signal if issuers collude

history.change: Privacy Sandbox wind down coverage; status of PST unverified
